_comment: Per-route, per-viewport byte budgets, UNCOMPRESSED. These match what inc/tools/audit.mjs measures, which is the dev server with no gzip or brotli. They are NOT what a visitor downloads: production serves mod_deflate + mod_brotli (.htaccess), and the text types compress roughly 5-6x. The phone homepage measures 479 KB here and lands near 245 KB over the wire.
_methodology: Re-baselined from scratch for the Machined Paper rebuild, from an actual measured run, not inherited. The previous budget was written against an architecture that no longer exists: it allowed 1250 KB of JS on a homepage whose note said it 'never loads three.js' (it did, via four separate focal devices) and 170 KB of images for 24 stock photographs that have since been deleted. Inheriting it would have meant the redesign passed a test of the thing it replaced.
_howToRead: budgetKB is a ceiling per resource type. Headroom is about 20% over the measured baseline: enough that a new icon or a paragraph does not fail the build, tight enough that a new dependency, an unoptimised image or a script that stopped being gated does.
_theOneThatMatters: phone / — total 600. Every other line is housekeeping; this one is the promise. three.js is gated OUT below 761px (js/stage3d.js checks matchMedia explicitly rather than relying on a CSS display:none, because a hidden canvas still costs the full download). If this line ever fails, that gate has broken, and the way it breaks is silent.

home.note: Desktop carries three.js (vendor/three/, ~750 KB uncompressed across two files) plus js/assembly.js and js/studio.js, loaded only after window load + requestIdleCallback and only on WebGL2, non-reduced-motion, non-Save-Data clients. Images are the pre-rendered object stills.

blog.note: Heaviest img figure of the default set: the listing page's article cover images.

default.note: No three.js anywhere. It used to load on all of these for a decorative object behind the page header; partials/head-object.php is now deliberately empty and records why. That single change is most of the 62% drop in secondary-page weight.
